meta.split_rule: Questions are numbered in book order; every 4th id (q04,q08,q12,q16,q20,q24) is test, the rest dev (18 dev / 6 test). Fixed before any run.
meta.filter_semantics: filter = {'chapter': N} is the user-supplied scope given in the question text ('In chapter N, ...'); it is an assumed input available before retrieval and is only applied by strategy C.
meta.leakage_risk: Single novel: dev and test share vocabulary, characters and style, so test is not independent of dev in topic; only the passages differ.

questions.question: Where did Mrs. Long say the young man who had taken Netherfield Park came from?
questions.expected_answer: From the north of England; he is described as a young man of large fortune.
questions.evidence_quote: a young man of large fortune from the north of England

questions.question: How did Mr. Darcy dismiss Elizabeth Bennet's looks when his friend suggested he dance with her?
questions.expected_answer: He said she was tolerable but not handsome enough to tempt him.
questions.evidence_quote: She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me

questions.question: What does Charlotte Lucas think about getting to know a person's character before marrying them?
questions.expected_answer: She thinks happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance, so knowing character beforehand does not help much.
questions.evidence_quote: Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.

questions.question: Why are the Bennet daughters unable to inherit their father's estate?
questions.expected_answer: The estate is entailed, in default of heirs male, on a distant relation.
questions.evidence_quote: an estate of two thousand a year, which, unfortunately for his daughters, was entailed, in default of heirs male, on a distant relation

alt_evidence.evidence_quote: I do think it is the hardest thing in the world, that your estate should be entailed away from your own children

questions.question: Why did Mrs. Bennet insist that Jane go to Netherfield on horseback rather than by carriage?
questions.expected_answer: Because it seemed likely to rain, so Jane would have to stay all night at Netherfield.
questions.evidence_quote: you had better go on horseback, because it seems likely to rain; and then you must stay all night

questions.question: Besides music, singing, drawing, dancing and the modern languages, what further quality does Mr. Darcy require of an accomplished woman?
questions.expected_answer: The improvement of her mind by extensive reading.
questions.evidence_quote: and to all she must yet add something more substantial in the improvement of her mind by extensive reading

questions.question: How does Mr. Darcy admit that his own temper falls short?
questions.expected_answer: He says he cannot vouch for his temper: it is too little yielding, too little for the convenience of the world.
questions.evidence_quote: My temper I dare not vouch for. It is, I believe, too little yielding; certainly too little for the convenience of the world.

questions.question: In chapter 16, what does Wickham say the late Mr. Darcy left him, and what happened to it?
questions.expected_answer: The next presentation of the best living in his gift; but when the living fell it was given elsewhere.
questions.evidence_quote: the late Mr. Darcy bequeathed me the next presentation of the best living in his gift. He was my godfather, and excessively attached to me. I cannot do justice to his kindness. He meant to provide for me amply, and thought he had done it; but when the living fell, it was given elsewhere.

questions.question: What was the third reason Mr. Collins gave for wishing to marry?
questions.expected_answer: It was the particular advice and recommendation of his noble patroness.
questions.evidence_quote: thirdly, which perhaps I ought to have mentioned earlier, that it is the particular advice and recommendation of the very noble lady whom I have the honour of calling patroness

questions.question: How does Elizabeth answer Mr. Collins when he suggests she may be waiting to be asked a second time?
questions.expected_answer: She says she is perfectly serious in her refusal: he could not make her happy and she would not make him happy.
questions.evidence_quote: I am perfectly serious in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who would make you so.

questions.question: Why did Charlotte Lucas accept Mr. Collins although she found him neither sensible nor agreeable?
questions.expected_answer: Marriage had always been her object: it was the only honourable provision for well-educated young women of small fortune.
questions.evidence_quote: Without thinking highly either of men or of matrimony, marriage had always been her object: it was the only honourable provision for well-educated young women of small fortune

questions.question: What did Colonel Fitzwilliam say Mr. Darcy had congratulated himself on?
questions.expected_answer: Having lately saved a friend from the inconveniences of a most imprudent marriage.
questions.evidence_quote: he congratulated himself on having lately saved a friend from the inconveniences of a most imprudent marriage

questions.question: In chapter 34, how does Mr. Darcy begin his declaration of love to Elizabeth?
questions.expected_answer: He says he has struggled in vain, his feelings will not be repressed, and he ardently admires and loves her.
questions.evidence_quote: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

questions.question: How does Elizabeth say the manner of Mr. Darcy's proposal affected her?
questions.expected_answer: It affected her only by sparing her the concern she might have felt in refusing him, had he behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.
questions.evidence_quote: You are mistaken, Mr. Darcy, if you suppose that the mode of your declaration affected me in any other way than as it spared me the concern which I might have felt in refusing you, had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner.

questions.question: In chapter 35, what did Wickham accept in return for resigning all claim to assistance in the church?
questions.expected_answer: Three thousand pounds.
questions.evidence_quote: He resigned all claim to assistance in the church, were it possible that he could ever be in a situation to receive it, and accepted in return three thousand pounds.

questions.question: How did Mr. Bennet respond to the plan of going to Brighton, and did Mrs. Bennet give up hope?
questions.expected_answer: He had no intention of yielding but gave vague and equivocal answers, so Mrs. Bennet, though often disheartened, never despaired of succeeding.
questions.evidence_quote: her father had not the smallest intention of yielding; but his answers were at the same time so vague and equivocal, that her mother, though often disheartened, had never yet despaired of succeeding at last

questions.question: How does Mrs. Reynolds describe her master, Mr. Darcy, as a landlord and as a master?
questions.expected_answer: The best landlord and the best master that ever lived.
questions.evidence_quote: He is the best landlord, and the best master," said she, "that ever lived.

questions.question: Where were Lydia and Wickham traced to after they left Brighton, and was Scotland their destination?
questions.expected_answer: They were traced almost to London but not beyond; they had certainly not gone to Scotland.
questions.evidence_quote: They left Brighton together on Sunday night, and were traced almost to London, but not beyond: they are certainly not gone to Scotland.

questions.question: What conditions did Mr. Gardiner say Mr. Bennet must meet so that Wickham would marry Lydia?
questions.expected_answer: Assure Lydia by settlement her equal share of the five thousand pounds secured among the children, and allow her one hundred pounds per annum during his life.
questions.evidence_quote: to assure to your daughter, by settlement, her equal share of the five thousand pounds, secured among your children after the decease of yourself and my sister; and, moreover, to enter into an engagement of allowing her, during your life, one hundred pounds per annum

questions.question: In chapter 56, how does Elizabeth reply when Lady Catherine presses her to promise never to engage herself to Mr. Darcy?
questions.expected_answer: She refuses to promise; she is resolved to act in the way that will constitute her own happiness, without reference to Lady Catherine.
questions.evidence_quote: I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.

alt_evidence.evidence_quote: I am not to be intimidated into anything so wholly unreasonable.

questions.question: What reason does Mr. Bennet give for enjoying gossip about his neighbours?
questions.expected_answer: He says we live to make sport for our neighbours and laugh at them in our turn.
questions.evidence_quote: For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?

questions.question: In chapter 58, how does Mr. Darcy renew his offer, and what does he say about his feelings since the spring?
questions.expected_answer: He says that if her feelings are still what they were last April she should tell him at once; his affections and wishes are unchanged, but one word from her will silence him for ever.
questions.evidence_quote: You are too generous to trifle with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. My affections and wishes are unchanged; but one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever.

questions.question: How long did Mr. Bingley and Jane remain at Netherfield after their marriage, and why did they leave?
questions.expected_answer: Only a twelvemonth; so near a vicinity to her mother and Meryton relations was not desirable.
questions.evidence_quote: Mr. Bingley and Jane remained at Netherfield only a twelvemonth. So near a vicinity to her mother and Meryton relations was not desirable even to his easy temper, or her affectionate heart.

questions.question: Why were Darcy and Elizabeth grateful to the Gardiners?
questions.expected_answer: Because they had been the means of uniting them by bringing her into Derbyshire.
questions.evidence_quote: they were both ever sensible of the warmest gratitude towards the persons who, by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them
